questions.q: On Oracle, what actually happens when you INSERT an empty string into a VARCHAR2 column?
options: Oracle stores it as NULL, not as a true empty string
Oracle stores it as an empty string, identical to T-SQL
Oracle rejects the INSERT with an error
Oracle converts it to the literal text 'NULL'
questions.explain: Oracle treats an empty VARCHAR2 as NULL at the storage level, so a WHERE column = '' check that works on T-SQL silently matches nothing on Oracle.

questions.q: Why is MySQL's historical leniency on type coercion still worth checking on a real production database today?
options: MySQL has never changed its default sql_mode in any version
Strict mode was removed from MySQL entirely
Plenty of production databases still run with a looser sql_mode inherited from an older install, even though current defaults are stricter
Type coercion only ever affects date columns
questions.explain: STRICT_TRANS_TABLES became part of the default sql_mode since MySQL 5.7, but older installs or inherited settings can still run looser -- so the actual sql_mode must be checked, not assumed.

questions.q: Why does quoting an identifier to preserve its exact mixed case become a liability when migrating from SQL Server to Oracle or PostgreSQL?
options: Quoting an identifier disables case folding on SQL Server
Quoted identifiers are automatically converted to lowercase on every platform
Once quoted, the exact case must be matched on every single reference afterward, forever
SQL Server does not support quoted identifiers at all
questions.explain: Oracle and PostgreSQL fold unquoted identifiers to a fixed case; quoting preserves exact case, but then that exact case is required on every future reference to the object.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the real risk with date/time values at migration time, beyond what Chapter 2 already covered?
options: Date values never need to be re-checked once Chapter 2 is understood
All four platforms store date/time values with identical precision
Only BIT columns are affected by precision differences
A value valid on the source platform is not guaranteed to be valid, or round the same way, on the target
questions.explain: Range and precision differences mean migration time is specifically when previously-valid values need re-checking against the target platform's actual limits.

questions.q: What is the real, consistent limitation of automated migration tools across platforms, per this lesson?
options: They only work on cloud warehouse platforms, never OLTP databases
They cannot translate any SQL at all without a human rewriting every line
They translate basic query syntax well but cannot reliably translate procedural logic like stored procedures, triggers, or packages
They translate procedural code perfectly but fail on basic SELECT statements
questions.explain: TRY/CATCH, EXCEPTION blocks, cursors, and dynamic SQL diverge too much across platforms for a tool to safely guess the correct rewrite every time -- human review is always needed for procedural objects.
